findings.text: Swift's single-line raw string `#"…"#` is set up as a fence, so an unclosed one stays open past the end of its line. In Swift (and by analogy with the goal's `"…"`, which ends on its line), only `#"""…"""#` spans lines. Example: `let r = #"abc` followed by `// note` counts the comment line as code, and every line after it stays a string until a `"#` turns up. Plain `"unclosed` is handled correctly and tested; the raw form is not.

The test named "takes a lifetime or a label for none" would also pass if `'` started a string running to the end of the line (or even to the next `'` on a later line). The lifetime and label lines (`fn f<'a>…`, `'outer: loop…`, `}`) are code either way, and no comment follows on the same or a later line. Add something that breaks a wrong reading, e.g. `fn f<'a>(x: &'a str) {} // c"` followed by a comment-only line, or `'a` followed later on the line by `"` or `/*`.

The goal's own nesting example, `/* a /* b */ still a comment */ let x = 1;`, is expected to count as code. It would count as code even if comments did not nest, because `let x` follows. Only lines 149–150 test nesting. The Swift test has the same problem at line 192. Use the example on its own as a comment-only line, or follow it with a line that depends on the comment having closed.

The Rust strings test never uses a raw string with no `#` (`r"…"` or `br"…"`), which the goal lists. Its byte string `b"/*"` (line 168) would also pass if `b"` were not recognised, because a plain `"` string covers it.

Two Swift rules the goal spells out are untested. First, inside `#"…"#` a backslash without the full count of `#` escapes nothing, e.g. `#"a\"# // c` must close at `"#`. Second, `#selector` (and `##` not followed by `"`) starts nothing. Only the `\#"` escape and `#if` are covered.

blind.summary: I found no blocker or major defect. Rust, Swift and Lua are mapped to the right names as sources. Nesting block comments (with their depth carried from line to line), Rust raw and byte strings, `'` character literals versus lifetimes, Swift's `"""` strings and `#` raw strings (including the rule that a backslash needs the full count of `#` to escape), Lua long comments and long strings with `=` counts, and `--[` falling back to a line comment all follow the goal. I checked this by reading the code and working through each test by hand; I did not run anything. The new `scan` gives the same results as the old `closeAt` for the other languages' strings, so they count as before. What's left is small: Swift's single-line raw strings carry over to the next line when left unclosed, and several tests can't fail for the reason their names give, or skip a rule the goal spells out.
